plan.contextChunk: This figure graphs a single upward-opening parabola on a coordinate plane and annotates its main features with labeled arrows. Both axes are numbered from -6 to 6 over a dotted gray grid, with x labeled at the right end of the horizontal axis and y at the top of the vertical one. The curve is a heavy teal U with arrowheads on both rising branches; its lowest point sits at x equal to 1, y equal to -4, and the branches climb to about y equal to 5 near x equal to -2 on the left and x equal to 4 on the right. Small filled dots mark the two crossings of the x-axis at x equal to -1 and x equal to 3, the crossing of the y-axis at y equal to -3, the turning point, and the mirror partner of the y-intercept at x equal to 2. A red dashed vertical line runs through x equal to 1, reached by an arrow from the label Axis of symmetry above. Three further labels point to the graph and read x-intercepts, y-intercept, and Vertex. Drawing the dashed line through the turning point lets the reader check that the marked dots sit at equal heights on either side. The graph fixes the vocabulary for reading a quadratic.

interactionPlan.concept: Every labeled feature of a quadratic graph — vertex, axis of symmetry, x- and y-intercepts, and the mirror point — is determined by just two things: the vertex location and the vertical stretch factor.

filled dot at x-intercept (3, 0)
filled dot at y-intercept (0, -3)
filled dot at vertex (1, -4)
filled dot at mirror point (2, -3), symmetric to the y-intercept across the axis
red dashed vertical line x = 1 (axis of symmetry)
label 'Axis of symmetry' with arrow pointing to the red dashed line
label 'x-intercepts' with arrows pointing to (-1,0) and (3,0)
label 'y-intercept' with arrow pointing to (0,-3)
label 'Vertex' with arrow pointing to (1,-4)

interactions.teaches: Dragging the lowest point moves the entire parabola rigidly: the red axis of symmetry slides to the new x-coordinate and the y-intercept/mirror pair re-form at equal heights on either side, so the single vertex fixes both the turning point and the line of symmetry.

interactions.label: Vertical stretch a
interactions.teaches: Changing the leading coefficient a widens or narrows the opening: the x-intercepts move symmetrically farther apart (small a) or closer together (large a) about the fixed axis, revealing how the quadratic coefficient controls intercept spacing while the vertex stays put.

interactions.label: Emphasize
interactions.teaches: Switching emphasis isolates the two vocabulary groups — the intercepts (where the curve crosses the axes) versus the symmetry set (vertex, axis line, and mirror point) — tying each term to a concrete visible feature of the graph.

demo_steps.title: Reading the parabola
demo_steps.narration: With a = 1 the curve is y = (x-1)^2 - 4: vertex (1,-4), x-intercepts at -1 and 3, y-intercept at -3, and its mirror at (2,-3). All four labels plus the red dashed axis are shown together as the standard vocabulary for a quadratic.

demo_steps.title: The vertex anchors symmetry
demo_steps.narration: Drag the vertex dot: the whole U translates, the red dashed axis of symmetry follows the new x-value, and the y-intercept and its mirror point reappear at matching heights on either side — the vertex alone fixes the turning point and the symmetry line.

demo_steps.title: Stretch moves the intercepts
demo_steps.narration: Return the vertex and sweep the stretch slider: the axis stays fixed while the two x-intercepts slide symmetrically apart (small a) or together (large a), showing the leading coefficient sets the opening width and hence the intercept spacing.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A parabola's entire labeled anatomy collapses to two parameters — the vertex (h,k) and the stretch a — because the axis of symmetry, both x-intercepts, the y-intercept, and its mirror point are all computed from y = a(x-h)^2 + k.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Center a square coordinate plane with both axes spanning -6..6, unit dotted gray grid behind. Draw the parabola as a thick teal U with small arrowheads on the upper ends of both branches; place solid dark dots at (-1,0), (3,0), (0,-3), (1,-4), (2,-3). Draw a red long-dashed vertical line through x=1 from top to bottom. Add four black text labels with thin leader arrows: 'Axis of symmetry' (top right, to the dashed line), 'x-intercepts' (right, splitting to the two axis crossings), 'y-intercept' (lower left, to (0,-3)), 'Vertex' (bottom right, to (1,-4)). When emphasizeToggle is 'Intercepts', brighten/enlarge the three intercept dots and dim the vertex/mirror/axis; when 'Symmetry', do the reverse; 'All' shows everything at equal weight. The curve, dots, dashed line, and intercept positions must recompute live from y = a(x-h)^2 + k as the vertex is dragged (h,k) or the slider changes a.

authoredContext:
The graph of a quadratic function is a U-shaped curve called a parabola. One important feature of the graph is that it has an extreme point, called the vertex. If the parabola opens up, the vertex represents the lowest point on the graph, or the minimum value of the quadratic function. If the parabola opens down, the vertex represents the highest point on the graph, or the maximum value. In either case, the vertex is a turning point on the graph. The graph is also symmetric with a vertical line drawn through the vertex, called the axis of symmetry. These features are illustrated in the figure.

Graph of a parabola showing where the x and y intercepts, vertex, and axis of symmetry are.

The y-intercept is the point at which the parabola crosses the y-axis. The x-intercepts are the points at which the parabola crosses the x-axis. If they exist, the x-intercepts represent the zeros, or roots, of the quadratic function, the values of x at which y=0.

discrepancies: The background grid is drawn as light dashed lines, whereas the source uses a fine dotted-point grid at integer intersections.
The parabola stroke is a green-teal (#0e7c7b) while the source curve is a steel/medium blue, a visible hue shift.
At higher stretch values the polyline is clamped flat against the top of the y-domain before the arrowheads are drawn, which can produce a short horizontal cap not present in the smooth source curve.
evaluation.notes: Structurally an excellent match: correct parabola y=(x-1)^2-4, vertex (1,-4), x-intercepts at -1 and 3, y-intercept (0,-3), mirror (2,-3), red dashed axis of symmetry, and all four leader-line labels are present and correctly placed; the stretch slider, emphasize radios, 3-step player, and draggable vertex are all functional and pedagogically tied to the concept. Main weaknesses are cosmetic: a green-teal curve instead of the source's blue and a dashed rather than dotted grid.
action_items: Change the parabola stroke (and its arrowheads) from #0e7c7b to a steel/medium blue (~#2f7fbf) to match the source curve color.
Render the grid as small dots at integer lattice points (e.g. tiny circles or a dot dasharray) instead of dashed lines to match the source's dotted grid.
Avoid clamping the polyline y-values to the domain top; instead stop adding points once y exceeds the domain so the curve exits the frame smoothly without a flat cap.
